slides.title: Data Representation
slides.body: Data Representation
slides.notes: Have you ever wondered what actually happens when you open an application, save a file, or run multiple programs at once? Throughout this course, we'll uncover the answers by exploring topics like Linux, processes, CPU scheduling, memory management, file systems, and I/O management. By the end, you'll have a clear understanding of how an Operating System manages the entire computer behind the scenes.

slides.title: Data Representation
slides.body:
How Computers See Information
Binary - Ones (1) and Zeros (0)
A binary number is a number expressed in Ones (1) and Zeros (0)
slides.notes: Moving on, have you ever wondered how computers understand information? They use the binary number system, where everything is represented using just 0s and 1s.

slides.title: Data Representation
slides.body:
Binary Representation
MSB(Most significant bit)
Example : Binary Representation of a number
LSB(Least significant bit)
slides.notes:
Next, let's understand a bit, the smallest unit of data, which can store either 0 or 1. In any binary number, the leftmost bit is called the Most Significant Bit (MSB), because it has the highest positional value.
The rightmost bit is called the Least Significant Bit (LSB), because it has the lowest positional value.
Now, let’s look at the example to clearly understand how MSB and LSB are identified in a binary number.

slides.title: Number Systems

slides.notes: Now we will be learning about the Number Systems.

Number System
A writing system for expressing numbers

slides.notes:
A number system is a writing system used to represent numbers using a set of symbols or digits.
Different number systems use different sets of symbols.
For example, the decimal system uses digits from 0 to 9, which is what we normally use in daily life.
In computing, we use other systems like binary, which uses only 0 and 1.

slides.title: Number System
slides.body:
Decimal Notation
4175
slides.notes: Next, let's start with the decimal number system, which we use in our daily lives. It uses the digits 0 to 9, and each digit's value depends on its position or place value.

slides.title: Number System
slides.body:
Radix / Base
NumberBase
Mathematical Representation
slides.notes: Now, what does the base or radix of a number system mean? It simply refers to the number of unique digits used in that system. For example, decimal has base 10, while binary has base 2.

slides.title: Number System
slides.body:
Number System

slides.notes: Moving on, computers work with the binary number system, which uses only 0 and 1. Just like decimal, the value of each bit depends on its position, as shown in the example.

slides.notes: So, can you spot the pattern? Just like decimal counting, binary also follows a sequence, but it uses only 0s and 1s to represent every number.

slides.title: Number System
slides.body:
Decimal to Binary Conversion
1310 = 11012
slides.notes: Moving on, how do we convert a decimal number into binary? We repeatedly divide the number by 2 and read the remainders from bottom to top to get the binary equivalent.

slides.title: Data Representation
slides.body:
Binary Representation
All types of content (text, images, videos and everything) must be converted to binary so that it can be stored by the computer
slides.notes: Now, regardless of whether it's text, an image, audio, or a video, every type of data is ultimately converted into binary before the computer can store or process it.

slides.title: Data Representation
slides.body:
Binary Representation
Different types of content occupy different amount of space in the computer because they are represented by different lengths of Binary number
slides.notes: Next, do all types of data occupy the same amount of storage? Not really. Different types of content require different amounts of space because they are represented using binary numbers of different lengths.

slides.title: Data Representation
slides.body:
Storing Integers in 4 Bits
4 bits = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 24 = 16
16 different types of information
A 4-bit number has 4 positions
Each position can be 0 or 1
slides.notes: What can we represent using 4 bits? Since each bit can be either 0 or 1, there are 2⁴, or 16 possible combinations. This means a 4-bit number can represent 16 different values, from 0 to 15.

slides.body:

slides.notes: Next, let's see what those 16 combinations actually represent. With 4 bits, we can store decimal numbers from 0 to 15, with each binary combination corresponding to one unique value.

slides.title: Data Representation
slides.body:
Binary Numbers
2n distinct combinations are possible
Can represent from 0  to  2n - 1
0 to 255 (28 - 1)

slides.notes: what happens when we increase the number of bits? An n-bit binary number can represent 2ⁿ combinations, ranging from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. For example, 8 bits represent 0 to 255, while 16 bits represent 0 to 65,535.

Different representations and conventions are developed to store different types of information
slides.notes: we've seen how positive numbers are stored, but what about negative numbers? For that, one bit is used to represent the sign—typically 0 for positive and 1 for negative—while the remaining bits represent the magnitude or value. We'll explore these representations in more detail next.

slides.notes: Next, let's understand this with an example. For +5, the sign bit is 0, followed by the binary value 101, giving 0101. For -5, only the sign bit changes to 1, while the magnitude remains the same, resulting in 1101.

slides.title: Images
slides.body: Representing Images
slides.notes: Moving on, have you ever wondered how a computer stores a picture like this? Just like numbers, images are also converted into binary so they can be stored, processed, and displayed by the computer.

slides.title: Representing Images
slides.body: Pixels
slides.notes: What makes up a digital image? It is made of tiny dots called pixels. When viewed closely, these individual pixels become visible, and together they form the complete image.

slides.title: Representing Images
slides.body:
Representing Colors
Each pixel has a specific color
Can use RGB model to represent colors
slides.notes: Every pixel has its own color. These colors are commonly represented using the RGB model, where different combinations of Red, Green, and Blue produce a wide range of colors.

slides.title: Data Representation
slides.body:
Representing Text
Each character is encoded as an integer which is represented by a binary value
slides.notes: Now, how is text stored inside a computer? Each character is assigned a unique integer value, which is then converted into binary. For example, the character 'A' is represented by the value 65.

slides.title: Data Representation
slides.body:
Basic Units of Data
Bit (b)
 Smallest unit of data → can be 0 or 1
Byte (B)
1 Byte = 8 bits
A byte can store one ASCII character
Larger Units
Kilobyte (KB) = 1024 Bytes
Megabyte (MB) = 1024 KB
Gigabyte (GB) = 1024 MB
Terabyte (TB) = 1024 GB
slides.notes: Finally, let's understand the basic units used to measure data. A bit is the smallest unit and can store either 0 or 1. Eight bits make one byte, which is enough to store a single ASCII character. As storage requirements grow, we use larger units such as KB, MB, GB, and TB.

slides.title: Character Encoding
slides.body: Character Encoding
slides.notes: Next,  we will learn about the Character Encoding

slides.title: Character Encoding
slides.body:
ASCII
American Standard Code for Information Interchange(ASCII)
Represents the English alphabet, digits, and punctuation marks
Requires only one byte to store a character
Uses 7 bits → 128 characters
slides.notes: Moving on, computers use ASCII, or American Standard Code for Information Interchange, to represent characters. It assigns a unique numeric value to English letters, digits, and special symbols. ASCII uses 7 bits, allowing it to represent 128 characters, and each character requires one byte of storage. For example, 'A' is 65, 'z' is 122, '1' is 49, and '*' is 42.

slides.title: Character Encoding
slides.body:
Unicode (Universal Character)
A
65
slides.notes: Next, what if we need to store characters from different languages or even emojis? That's where Unicode comes in. Unlike ASCII, it supports far more than 128 characters and uses more than one byte when needed, making it suitable for representing text from languages around the world.

slides.title: Unicode
slides.body:
UTF-8
UTF-8 (Unicode Transformation Format - 8)
Capable of storing 1,112,064 different characters
Has same values for ASCII characters
"A" 
Unicode code point - 65
"z" 
Unicode - 122
"1" 
Unicode - 49
"*" 
Unicode - 42
slides.notes: Moving on, UTF-8, or Unicode Transformation Format-8, is the most widely used Unicode encoding. It can represent over 1.1 million characters, making it suitable for storing text from different languages, symbols, and emojis. Another advantage is that it uses the same code values as ASCII for standard characters, so 'A' is 65, 'z' is 122, '1' is 49, and '*' is 42.

slides.title: Character Encoding
slides.body:
UTF-8

slides.notes: one of the biggest advantages of UTF-8 is that it can represent characters from different languages as well as emojis. Every character is assigned a unique Unicode code point, allowing computers to identify and display it correctly, regardless of the language or symbol being used.

slides.title: Data Representation
slides.body: Binary Representation
slides.notes:
Binary is represented in computers using electrical signals controlled by transistors.
These transistors work by switching between two voltage levels: high and low.
We can imagine this using a simple example like a light bulb and a switch.
When the light is ON, we represent it as 1, and when it is OFF, we represent it as 0.
This is how computers use binary to represent and process information.
